tip: Russian says have with у (u) plus genitive: у моего брата есть собака (u mayevo brata yest sabaka = my brother has a dog).
вместо (vmesta = instead of) takes the genitive: вместо чая (vmesta chaya), чай (chay) becoming чая.
то ли... то ли (to li... to li) means either... or with a note of uncertainty: то ли дождь (dozhd = rain), то ли снег (sneg = snow).
The preposition sits before который (katoryy = which): на котором мы ехали (na katoram my yekhali = on which we rode), not который alone up front.
чей (chey = whose) agrees with the thing owned: чей ребёнок (rebyonak = child) is masculine; use чья (chya) for feminine, чьё (chyo) for neuter.
A comparative plus всех (vsekh = of all) makes a superlative: вкуснее всех (vkusnee vsekh = tastier than all), meaning the tastiest.
худший (khudshiy = worst) is the one-word superlative of плохой (plakhoy = bad); лучший (luchshiy) is its opposite, best.
такой же... как (takoy zhe... kak) means as... as, showing equality: такая же умная, как мама (takaya zhe umnaya, kak mama = as smart as mom).
чем... тем (chem... tem) means the more X, the more Y: чем раньше встанешь, тем больше успеешь (chem ranshe vstanesh, tem bolshe uspeesh).
Possessives match the noun owned, not the owner. окно (akno = window) is neuter, so моё (mayo = my), not мой (moy) or моя (maya).
чей (chey = whose) agrees with the owned thing. зонт (zont = umbrella) is masculine, so чей; a feminine noun takes чья (chya).
свою (svayu = his own) points back to the subject: любит свою работу (lyubit svayu rabotu = loves his own job); его (yevo) could mean someone else's.
его (yevo = his) never changes form. Whatever the noun's gender or case, it stays его: его работа (rabota = work).
нравится (nravitsya = is pleasing) puts the liker in the dative: моим родителям (maim raditelyam = my parents). The thing liked is the grammatical subject.
гордиться (garditsya = to be proud) takes the instrumental with no preposition: гордимся своим городом (gardimsya svaim goradam = we're proud of our city).
Times of day take the instrumental, no preposition: утром (utram = in the morning), from утро (utra). Likewise вечером (vecheram), днём (dnyom), ночью (nochyu).
скучать (skuchat = to miss) uses по (pa) plus the dative: скучаем по своему дому (skuchaem pa svayemu domu = we miss our home).
то, что (to, chto = what) joins a main clause to a relative one: то (to) sits first, что (chto) opens the second, as in то, что мне нужно (mne nuzhna = I need).
чей (chey) also serves as relative 'whose', agreeing with the owned noun: собака, чей хозяин ушёл (sabaka, chey khazyain ushyol = the dog whose owner left).
When the subject stays the same, чтобы (chtoby) takes an infinitive: позвонил, чтобы узнать (pazvanil, chtoby uznat = called to find out).
ни ... ни (ni ... ni = neither ... nor) still needs a negated verb: ни он, ни она не знали (ni on, ni ana ne znali = neither he nor she knew).
вместо того чтобы (vmesta tavo chtoby = instead of) is followed by an infinitive, here отдыхать (atdykhat = to rest).
а (a) joins clauses with a light contrast, softer than 'but': звонил, а никто не ответил (zvanil, a nikto ne atvetil = called, but nobody answered).
который (katoryy = which) takes gender from the noun it replaces but case from its own clause: дом (dom = house) is masculine, and в (v = in) makes it prepositional: в котором (v katoram).
Russian uses the future in both halves of a real future condition: поедем, если будет (payedem, yesli budet = we'll go if it is), where English keeps the present.
с собой (s saboy = with oneself) is the reflexive 'with him/her': носит с собой (nosit s saboy = carries with him).
мало того что (mala tavo chto = not only that) sets up an added point, often paired with ещё и (yeshchyo i = and also).
For places, где (gde = where) can replace в котором (v katoram): город, где я родился (gorad, gde ya radilsya = the city where I was born).
After кто (kto = who) the verb stays singular even for many people: тех, кто помог (tekh, kto pamog = those who helped), not помогли (pamagli).
словно (slovna = as if) introduces an unreal comparison: говорила так, словно знала всё (gavarila tak, slovna znala vsyo = spoke as if she knew everything).
